source.author: Al Brooks
source.chapter_title: Part II: Magnets: Support and Resistance

conventions: stop entries mechanized as signal-bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode

candidates.name: PriorDayExtremeLevel
candidates.quote: Yesterday's high, low, open, and close.
candidates.description: Shared primitive: the prior session's high, low, open, or close acts as a support/resistance magnet level for the current session.
candidates.pseudocode: priorDayHigh = highest(high, sessionBars)[sinceSessionStart]; abs(close[0] - priorDayHigh) <= toleranceTicks * tickSize
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (level construction; used as a target/reversal-area test)
notes: Chapter 10 (Other Magnets) is expected to give the canonical, fuller treatment of this and the other list items below.

candidates.name: DailyPivotLevel
candidates.description: Shared primitive: the classic floor-trader daily pivot, (priorDayHigh + priorDayLow + priorDayClose) / 3, acts as a support/resistance magnet.
candidates.pseudocode: pivot = (priorDayHigh + priorDayLow + priorDayClose) / 3; abs(close[0] - pivot) <= toleranceTicks * tickSize

complexity.reason: Brooks names 'daily pivots' without specifying which formula (classic/Woodie/Camarilla); a design decision is needed

candidates.name: FibonacciRetracementLevel
candidates.description: Shared primitive: a Fibonacci retracement/projection ratio (e.g., 38.2%, 50%, 61.8%) of the most recent swing acts as a support/resistance magnet.
candidates.pseudocode: swingHigh = mostRecentSwingHigh(pivotStrength); swingLow = mostRecentSwingLow(pivotStrength); level = swingHigh - fibRatio * (swingHigh - swingLow); abs(close[0] - level) <= toleranceTicks * tickSize

complexity.reason: needs swing-pivot detection to anchor the retracement, and which ratio to use is itself a choice

notes: Book merely lists this as a common S/R type; gives no worked example in this chapter.

candidates.name: TradeTowardUnreachedMagnetOnlyFilter
candidates.quote: When you become aware of a magnet not too far from the current price, trade only in the direction of the magnet until after it is reached.
candidates.description: Filter: while a known price magnet lies within magnetRangeTicks ahead in the current direction and has not yet been touched, permit only entries toward that magnet; block fresh countertrend entries until it is reached.
candidates.pseudocode: distanceToMagnet = abs(nearestUnreachedMagnetLevel - close[0]); distanceToMagnet <= magnetRangeTicks * tickSize && !magnetReachedYet => blockCountertrendEntry

complexity.reason: requires a design decision on which remembered levels qualify as 'the' magnet and how 'reached' is defined

notes: Book immediately qualifies this: 'there still can be reliable trades in both directions' before the magnet is reached, so this is a soft bias, not a hard block.

candidates.name: WeakMoveTowardMagnetAgainstTrendFade
candidates.quote: If the move toward the magnet is weak and if it is against the direction of a larger trend, you can also look to initiate a trade in the opposite direction, expecting a reversal.
candidates.description: When price approaches a known magnet counter to the larger trend with weak (small-bodied, overlapping) bars, enter with the larger trend expecting a reversal at the magnet.
candidates.pseudocode: distanceToMagnet <= magnetRangeTicks * tickSize && avgBodyFraction(recentBars) <= weakBodyFraction && counterToLargerTrend

complexity.reason: needs a magnet level, a larger-trend-context read, and a 'weak move' bar-quality test together

candidates.name: SecondReversalAtMagnetEntry
candidates.quote: If the trend resumes and goes even further past the magnet and then reverses a second time, this is usually a reliable setup for a trade in the opposite direction, especially if there is a strong reversal bar.
candidates.description: After price first overshoots a magnet and reverses, then resumes and overshoots the magnet a second time, a strong reversal bar on the second overshoot is a reliable countertrend entry.
candidates.book_order_type: stop entry beyond the second reversal bar

complexity.reason: needs a remembered magnet level and a persistent count of prior overshoot-and-reversal events at it

notes: A magnet-specific instance of the general 'second entries are more reliable' idea also seen in Chapter 5 (double top/bottom, H2/L2).

candidates.name: SupportWeakensAfterRepeatedTestsFilter
candidates.quote: In general, if the market tests an area of support four or five times, the likelihood of breaking through that support increases and, at some point, the breakout becomes more likely than not.
candidates.description: Filter: count touches of a support/resistance level within toleranceTicks over lookback bars; once the touch count reaches touchesForWeakening, reduce confidence that the level will keep holding (favor a breakout trade over another bounce trade).
candidates.pseudocode: touchCount = countBarsWithin(level, toleranceTicks, lookback); touchCount >= touchesForWeakening => favorBreakoutOverBounce

complexity.reason: a window loop counting proximity touches of a remembered level

notes: Illustrated in the chapter with a flat moving average that stops attracting buyers after repeated failed touches.

candidates.name: SupportResistanceRoleFlipPrimitive
candidates.quote: Once the market falls through support, it usually becomes resistance; and once the market breaks above resistance, it usually becomes support.
candidates.description: Shared primitive: once a remembered support level is broken (closed below), relabel it as a resistance level for future tests from below (and mirror for resistance broken to the upside).
candidates.pseudocode: if wasSupport(level) && close[0] < level - toleranceTicks * tickSize: level.role = resistance
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (level-state transition, feeds other S/R-based rules)

complexity.reason: needs a persistent level object with a role flag that flips on a qualifying break

notes: Applies to any of the level primitives above (moving average, trend line, trading-range boundary, etc.).

candidates.name: SlopingChannelCounterFlagBias
candidates.quote: any upward-sloping channel should be thought of as a bear flag, even if it is part of a bull market, because eventually there will be a break below the trend line and the market will behave as if the channel was a bear flag for trading purposes. Likewise, any downward-sloping channel should be thought of as a bull flag
candidates.description: Filter/context: regardless of the larger trend, treat any currently rising channel as a bear flag (expect an eventual downside break to trade) and any falling channel as a bull flag (expect an eventual upside break to trade).
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (context filter shaping which breakout to trade)

complexity.reason: needs channel-line detection and a persistent slope read

candidates.name: TakeProfitAtInitialRiskMultiple
candidates.quote: the reward has to be at least as large as the risk to create a positive trader's equation. This usually results in some profit taking once the reward reaches the size of the risk
candidates.description: Take (partial) profits once open profit reaches at least riskMultiple times the position's initial risk (entry price minus the initial protective stop).
candidates.pseudocode: initialRisk = abs(ctx.EntryPrice() - ctx.InitialStopPrice()); ctx.OpenPositionProfit() >= riskMultiple * initialRisk
candidates.book_order_type: profit-taking limit at 1R (or riskMultiple x R)

complexity.reason: needs the position's initial stop distance remembered, not just a fixed dollar amount like TakeProfit

notes: Unlike TakeProfitWithRatioStop (fixed dollar target with a stop expressed as a ratio of it), this scales the profit target off the trade's own actual initial risk, which varies by placement.

candidates.name: TopsFromRangesBottomsFromClimaxesFilter
candidates.quote: Most major tops do not come from climaxes made of huge bars and volume, which are more common at major bottoms. More often, a top comes from a trading range, like a double top or a head and shoulders top, followed by a breakout in the form of a bear spike.
candidates.description: Context asymmetry filter: weight climax-based reversal entries (large trend bars, exhaustion gaps) more heavily near suspected bottoms, and weight range/double-top/head-and-shoulders breakout-failure entries more heavily near suspected tops.
candidates.pseudocode: if searchingForBottom: preferSignal(ClimaxReversalEntry) else if searchingForTop: preferSignal(DoubleTopOrRangeBreakoutFailureEntry)

complexity.reason: 'major top' vs 'major bottom' identification is itself a design decision; this is an asymmetry heuristic, not a standalone testable trigger

notes: Book explicitly hedges: 'tops can be climactic, and bottoms can be trading ranges' — this is a tendency, not a rule.

rejected.quote: computer algorithms, which generate 70 percent of all trading volume and 80 percent of institutional volume
rejected.reason: descriptive market-structure statistic, not data the engine has or a bar-level test

rejected.quote: When a reporter takes a cab to work and the driver tells him that he just sold all of his stocks and mortgaged his house so that he could buy gold...
rejected.reason: news/sentiment anecdote; no bar-level test and no news data available to the engine

rejected.quote: The fundamentals (the value in buying or selling) determine the overall direction, but the technicals determine the actual turning points.
rejected.reason: fundamental/institutional-flow narrative with no OHLCV-decidable condition

chapter_summary: Part II's introduction is almost entirely conceptual scaffolding for the magnets/support-resistance framework used throughout the rest of the book (institutions, HFT, vacuums, fundamentals vs. technicals) and is mostly not mechanizable; the bulk of it is rejected or only noted. It does contribute a catalog of magnet types (several new: yesterday's OHLC, daily pivots, Fibonacci levels), a support/resistance role-flip primitive (broken support becomes resistance and vice versa) that other chapters' filters can build on, a repeated-test-weakens-the-level filter, a magnet-overshoot/second-reversal entry pattern, a directional-bias-toward-an-unreached-magnet filter, a risk-multiple profit-taking Exit distinct from the catalog's fixed-dollar TakeProfit rules, and a channel-slope-implies-opposite-flag heuristic. Everything here is graded research/hard/moderate; Chapter 10 (Other Magnets) is explicitly the fuller, presumably more concrete treatment of the level catalog and should be checked by the dedup pass.
